title: Managing triplet lambs
subtitle: Keeping all three alive when a ewe cannot raise all her lambs unaided.
excerpt: A ewe carrying triplets delivers three lambs but typically has enough milk for two. The third lamb, usually the smallest, is at high risk of starvation within the first 48 hours unless you intervene. The options are: select the smallest triplet and adopt it onto a ewe that has lost a lamb, move it to an artificial rearing system, or supplement it while leaving all three with the mother. Which works depends on what resources you have at lambing time.
sourceNotes: AHDB Beef and Lamb, Better Returns Programme: Sheep BRP Manual 1 (2022), triplet management section. Moredun Research Institute, Multiple-bearing ewe management (2021). DEFRA Code of Recommendations for the Welfare of Sheep (2018). SAC Consulting, Lambing Management Guide (2021).

glossaryTerms.definition: Raising a lamb on milk replacer fed via an ad-lib teat bucket or automatic feeder, without a ewe foster mother. Lambs raised artificially are called 'pet lambs' and must be fed four to six times daily until weaned onto creep feed and grass.

Transferring a lamb onto a ewe that is not its dam, usually by masking its scent to match the ewe's own lamb. Common methods include covering the foster lamb in the amniotic fluid or membranes of the ewe's own lamb, or using a skin graft from a dead lamb.

The first milk produced by the ewe, essential for immune transfer. In triplets, the key rule is that all three lambs must receive colostrum in the first two hours of life before any decision is made about which lamb to remove or foster.

content.text: When a ewe lambs with triplets, the priority in the first two hours is to get
colostrum

into all three lambs before making any decision about which lamb to remove. Tube-feed any lamb that is not actively suckling: all three must have their first colostrum dose regardless of what happens next. Once colostrum is in, you have a few hours to make decisions.
The options
Foster the weakest or smallest lamb onto a ewe that has lost a lamb, or onto a ewe with a single lamb that can accept a second.
Remove the smallest lamb and raise it artificially on milk replacer.
Leave all three with the ewe and supplement the smallest with bottle feeds or tube feeds until the ewe's milk supply increases over the first two weeks.

Fostering is the best outcome for the lamb if a suitable recipient ewe is available. An artificially reared lamb grows well but requires significant labour for the first six weeks. If you run a small flock, a single pet lamb in the house is manageable; in a larger system, an automatic ad-lib feeder handles ten to twenty lambs without constant attention.
Fostering onto another ewe
Ewes identify their own lambs by scent. Fostering (also called
adoption
) works by masking the smell of the incoming lamb:

The most reliable method is to use the amniotic membranes or fluid from the recipient ewe's own delivery, covering the foster lamb with them. This works within the first two to four hours after birth when the ewe is still in bonding mode.
If the ewe's lamb was stillborn, skin the dead lamb and fit the skin as a jacket over the foster lamb. Leave in place for two to three days until the ewe accepts the lamb fully by scent.
Confine the ewe and foster lamb in a small pen (1.5 m by 1.5 m) together for 2 to 3 days. In a tight pen the ewe cannot easily move away and nursing becomes routine.
Watch for the ewe head-butting or repeatedly rejecting the foster lamb. If she is consistently violent after 48 hours, move to the artificial rearing option.
Artificial rearing
For
artificial rearing

. Mix lamb milk replacer to the manufacturer's dilution and feed 200 to 250 ml five times daily in the first week. Drop to three or four times daily by week two as the lamb starts nibbling creep feed. Ad-lib warm milk via a teat bucket is an option once the lamb drinks reliably.

attrs.cue: Fostered lamb keeps getting pushed out by the ewe's own lamb
attrs.cause: Ewe's own lamb is dominant and prevents the foster lamb from accessing the udder
attrs.fix: Rotate access for feeding sessions: physically block the own lamb for 15 minutes while the foster lamb suckles, twice daily. Over a week, the ewe's routine adapts to feeding both.

attrs.cue: Artificially reared lamb scouring on milk replacer
attrs.cause: Milk replacer made too strong, fed too cold, or lamb drinking too much too fast
attrs.fix: Recheck dilution against the product instructions. Milk must be fed at 38 to 40 degrees. Use a slow-flow teat if the lamb is draining a bottle in under 90 seconds.
